implementation_notes: Java specifies lazy class initialization: a class is initialized immediately before its first active use (instance creation, static field access, static method invocation, reflection) under a unique per-class initialization lock, so a static final field initialized in its declaration is constructed exactly once at exactly the right moment and the C++ problem does not exist. The structural form of this idiom is the initialization-on-demand holder: a private static nested class holds the instance and is only initialized when first referenced. Thread safety comes from the JVM's class-initialization protocol, not from locks in the source; the only thing to avoid is initialization cycles.
pitfalls: Constant variables (static final with a compile-time constant initializer) are inlined by the compiler and do not trigger class initialization at all, so a class whose only 'use' is such a constant may never run its initializer - use a holder or a non-constant initializer when that matters.
Initialization failure is permanent: the class is marked erroneous, the failure surfaces as ExceptionInInitializerError (or NoClassDefFoundError on later access) and no retry happens.

Mutually dependent classes initialized by two threads can deadlock on the two initialization locks, and subclass initialization that reads overridden state can observe a superclass field before it is set.
Class initialization is triggered indirectly as well (subclass initialization, reflection with initialize=true); Class.forName(name, false, loader) is the escape hatch when it must not run.
